source: This replacement is also mirrored in part in γδ T cells in the dermis, where an IL-17-secreting subset (Tγδ17) develops before birth and is self-renewing, in contrast to IFN-γ–producing CD27+γδ T cells, which are constantly replenished by newly generated γδ-T cells from the thymus (Sandrock et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In the adult lung, local immune defense is mainly provided by tissue-resident macrophages, including interstitial macrophages (IM) and alveolar macrophages (AM).
source: In the adult lung, local immune defense is mainly provided by tissue-resident MΦ. Two main sets of tissue-resident MΦ can be distinguished, interstitial MΦ (IM) and alveolar MΦ (AM) (Evren et al., 2020; Kopf et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In the fetal and newborn mouse, the lung immune defense system is established by tissue-resident macrophages via several waves of cell recruitment.
source: In the fetal and newborn mouse, the lung immune defense system is established by tissue-resident MΦ via several waves of cell recruitment (Evren et al., 2020; Kopf et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The first wave of lung macrophages consists of yolk sac-derived macrophages, which can be detected in the lung from around E10 and are characterized by high expression of F4/80 and low expression of CD11b.
source: The first wave consists of YS-derived MΦ, which can be detected in the lung from around E10. These MΦ have a heterogeneous shape with multiple pseudopods and are characterized by high expression of F4/80 and low expression of CD11b.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the first wave of lung macrophages.

claim: The second wave of macrophage recruitment to the lung consists of fetal liver-derived monocytes, which appear in the lung at E12 and exhibit a round cell shape, low expression of F4/80, and high expression of CD11b.
source: The second wave of MΦ recruitment to the lung consists of fetal liver-derived monocytes, which appear in the lung at E12. These MΦ exhibit a round cell shape, low expression of F4/80, and high expression of CD11b (Guilliams et al., 2013; Hashimoto et al., 2013; Tan and Krasnow, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Both yolk sac-derived and fetal liver-derived macrophage populations are distributed diffusely in the fetal lung interstitium between E14 and 17.
source: Both populations are distributed diffusely in the fetal lung interstitium between E14 and 17 (Tan and Krasnow, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The first wave of yolk sac-derived resident macrophages does not substantially proliferate and remains as interstitial macrophages in the interstitial space, and postnatally these cells are continuously renewed by circulating bone marrow-derived monocytes.
source: The first wave of YS-derived resident MΦ does not substantially proliferate and remains as IM in the interstitial space. Postnatally, these cells are continuously renewed by circulating bone marrow-derived monocytes.
evidence: This describes the fate of yolk sac-derived lung macrophages.

claim: The second wave of macrophages shows strong proliferative activity starting at E16 in the lung interstitium, leading to the establishment of alveolar macrophages, which start to develop around birth in the mouse.
source: The second wave of MΦ shows strong proliferative activity starting at E16 in the lung interstitium, leading to the establishment of the uniquely localized alveolar MΦ, which – in the mouse – start to develop around birth.
evidence: This describes the development of alveolar macrophages.

claim: Fetal monocytes outcompete yolk sac macrophages in the development to alveolar macrophages late in fetal development, which has lasting consequences for proper lung function and immune defense.
source: In other words, fetal monocytes outcompete YS MΦ in the development to alveolar MΦ late in fetal development, which has lasting consequences for proper lung function and immune defense (Guilliams et al., 2013; Li et al., 2020; Tan and Krasnow, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The third wave of lung macrophages is recruited from bone marrow-derived circulating monocytes starting immediately after birth to fill up any niche of interstitial macrophages throughout postnatal life.
source: The third wave of lung MΦ is recruited to the lung from bone marrow-derived circulating monocytes starting immediately after birth to fill up any niche of interstitial MΦ throughout postnatal life.
evidence: This describes the third wave of lung macrophage recruitment.

claim: Similar mechanisms concerning ontogeny of tissue-resident macrophages may also apply for the development of interstitial and alveolar macrophages during human ontogeny.
source: Similar mechanisms concerning ontogeny of tissue-resident MΦ may also apply for the development of interstitial and alveolar MΦ during human ontogeny, as addressed in a recently published study (Evren et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Alveolar macrophages play a central role in the immediate postnatal protection of the lung from infections.

evidence: This describes the functional importance of alveolar macrophages.

claim: Alveolar macrophages exhibit a unique territorial behavior with on average three alveoli being surveilled by one alveolar macrophage.

claim: The positioning of prealveolar macrophages to the alveoli and the cell-intrinsic transition to alveolar macrophages require the actin-bundling protein L-plastin.
source: Yet, the positioning of prealveolar MΦ to the alveoli and the cell-intrinsic transition to AM appear to require the actin-bundling protein L-plastin (Todd et al., 2016).

claim: Alveolar macrophage positioning and transition depends on GM-CSF produced by alveolar epithelial cells.

claim: Alveolar macrophages keep their capacity for self-renewal throughout postnatal life.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

source: Yet, they can be replaced by circulating monocytes in cases of severe damage to the alveolar MΦ population, for example, after infection or lung irradiation therapy (Machiels et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

evidence: This is an inference about the vulnerability of the developing lung.

source: Microglial progenitor differentiation from early EMPs in the YS relies on cell-intrinsic programs, in particular driven by transcription factors, for example, Sfpi/Pu.1 and Irf8 (Matcovitch-Natan et al., 2016; Thion et al., 2018; Kierdorf et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Sfpi/Pu.1-deficient mice do not have any microglia in the CNS parenchyma.
source: Sfpi/Pu.1-deficient mice do not have any microglia in the CNS parenchyma
evidence: This describes the phenotype of Sfpi/Pu.1-deficient mice.

claim: Irf8-deficient mice show a reduced number of progenitors and embryonic microglia.
source: whereas Irf8-deficient mice show a reduced number of progenitors and embryonic microglia (Kierdorf et al., 2013).

source: Adult Irf8-deficient mice have an altered number of microglia in the parenchyma and show severe maturation defects (Hagemeyer et al., 2016).

claim: The CSF1 receptor has two ligands, IL-34 and CSF1, both expressed in the CNS with a spatially distinct expression pattern that establishes postnatally.

claim: Gray matter microglia depend predominantly on IL-34 produced by neurons, while white matter microglia depend on CSF1 secreted by astrocytes during postnatal phases and adulthood.
source: As an example, gray matter microglia depend predominantly on IL-34 produced by neurons, while white matter microglia depend on CSF1 secreted by astrocytes during postnatal phases and adulthood (Kana et al., 2019).

source: Besides CSF1 and IL-34, microglial expansion and homeostasis is highly dependent on TGF-β. Loss of TGF-β signaling in adult microglia results in a hyperactivated phenotype and disturbance of homeostasis (Butovsky et al., 2014; Zöller et al., 2018).

claim: Loss of TGF-β signaling during microglial development results in impairment of microglial expansion throughout the developing CNS.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Microglial homeostasis and development are highly influenced by external environmental cues, with one example being the dependence of microglial maturation on the gut microbiota.
source: Even though microglia reside behind the closed blood-brain barrier (BBB) within the CNS parenchyma and are shielded early on during development, microglial homeostasis and development are also highly influenced by external environmental cues with one interesting example being the dependence of microglial maturation on the gut microbiota.

claim: Germ-free mice show a maturation defect of adult microglia, resulting in an altered reaction to inflammatory cues such as lipopolysaccharides (LPS).

claim: Microglial sensing of the microbiota provides essential signals during development.
source: Therefore, microglial sensing of the microbiota seems to provide essential signals during development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evidence about germ-free mice.

claim: Microbiota-derived signals highly affect microglia in postnatal development, whereas embryonic microglia until birth is less affected by the absence of the microbiota.
source: Microbiota-derived signals highly affect microglia in postnatal development, whereas embryonic microglia until birth is less affected by the absence of the microbiota (Thion et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Microglial development is shaped by different cues derived from the CNS and the peripheral environment.
source: Microglial development is shaped by different cues derived from the CNS but also the peripheral environment.
evidence: This is a summary statement about factors influencing microglial development.

claim: The perinatal phase is an important time for CNS immune development and maturation, and postnatal microglia serve a plethora of different functions and are very dynamic in terms of mobility and proliferation.
source: Especially during and shortly after birth manifold changes are seen in the transcriptional differentiation program of microglia. Therefore, the perinatal phase is an important time for CNS immune development and maturation. Furthermore, postnatal microglia are serving a plethora of different functions and are very dynamic in terms of mobility and proliferation, making insults in their developmental program detrimental for the CNS during this vulnerable phase.
evidence: This is a synthesis statement about the importance of the perinatal phase for microglial development.

claim: The intestinal mucosa transits from sterility before birth to being densely colonized by commensal bacteria and threatened by enteropathogens after birth.
source: The intestinal mucosa transits from sterility – and thus largely deprived from microbial innate immune stimuli – before birth to being densely colonized by commensal bacteria, and threatened by enteropathogens after birth.
evidence: This describes the transition of the intestinal mucosa at birth.

claim: With the introduction of solid food, the intestinal mucosa is additionally subjected to a large variety of dietary antigens.
source: With the introduction of solid food, the intestinal mucosa is additionally subjected to a large variety of dietary antigens.
evidence: This describes an additional challenge for the intestinal mucosa.

claim: The parallel exposure to food and microbiota is beneficial since microorganisms in neonatal gastrointestinal tract improve energy harvesting for growth.
source: The parallel exposure to food and microbiota is beneficial since microorganisms in neonatal gastrointestinal tract improve energy harvesting for growth (Ganal-Vonarburg et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The neonatal intestinal mucosa has to endure bacterial colonization and prevent inappropriate inflammation, direct bacterial composition of a beneficial microbiota, generate and maintain adaptive immune tolerance to dietary and microbial antigens, and establish innate and adaptive antimicrobial host reactivity to overcome challenges by enteropathogens.
source: On the other hand, the challenges for the neonatal intestinal mucosa are tremendous since it has to (i) endure bacterial colonization and prevent inappropriate inflammation, (ii) direct bacterial composition of a beneficial microbiota, (iii) generate and maintain adaptive immune tolerance to dietary and microbial antigens, and (iv) establish innate and adaptive antimicrobial host reactivity to overcome challenges by enteropathogens.
evidence: This lists the challenges faced by the neonatal intestinal mucosa.

claim: A timed succession of non-redundant phases facilitates postnatal immune development and the step-by-step establishment of mucosal homeostasis.
source: A timed succession of non-redundant phases facilitates postnatal immune development and the step-by-step establishment of mucosal homeostasis (Hornef and Torow, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Microbiota-immune interactions starting immediately after birth have been implicated in a variety of both 'non-communicable' gastrointestinal diseases, like inflammatory bowel disease, as well as extraintestinal disorders ranging from psoriasis to rheumatic arthritis, metabolic syndrome, neurodegeneration, and cancer.
source: Moreover, microbiota-immune interactions starting immediately after birth have been implicated in a variety of both 'non-communicable' gastrointestinal diseases, like inflammatory bowel disease, as well as extraintestinal disorders ranging from psoriasis to rheumatic arthritis, metabolic syndrome, neurodegeneration, and cancer.
evidence: This describes the broad implications of early microbiota-immune interactions.

claim: A causal link between early microbiota-immune interactions and various diseases has not been firmly established in all cases.
source: Notably, a causal link has not been firmly established in all cases (Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research and acknowledges uncertainty.

claim: The healthy fetal intestine is sterile, albeit low levels of microbial constituents derived from the maternal microbiota reach the neonate and contribute to early immune priming.

claim: With rupture of the amniotic membranes, the neonatal organism gets into contact with the bacteria colonizing the maternal vaginal and gastrointestinal tract.
source: With rupture of the amniotic membranes, the neonatal organism gets into contact with the bacteria colonizing the maternal vaginal and gastrointestinal tract (Ganal-Vonarburg et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Maternal fecal bacteria represent the dominant source of neonatal microbiota in vaginally delivered neonates, whereas C-section is associated with a more environment- or skin-like neonatal microbiota.
source: Whereas maternal fecal bacteria represent the dominant source in vaginally delivered neonates, C-section is associated with a more environment- or skin-like neonatal microbiota (Dominguez-Bello et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Upon initial exposure, bacterial density quickly reaches threshold levels.
source: Upon initial exposure, bacterial density quickly reaches threshold levels (van Best et al., 2020a).

source: In humans, it requires 2–3 years after birth for bacterial diversity and composition to reach adult levels and stability (Bäckhed et al., 2015; Yatsunenko et al., 2012).

source: Whereas microbial antigens are already present in the intestinal lumen at high concentrations early after birth, direct exposure to dietary non-self antigens starts later, in particular with the introduction of solid food.

source: For example, shortly after birth the epithelium undergoes reprogramming and thus acquires innate immune tolerance via miR-146a-mediated translational repression of the TLR signaling molecule IL-1 receptor-associated kinase 1 (Lotz et al., 2006; Chassin et al., 2010).
